questions.q: What should people do when they go to the house of God?
questions.a: They should be careful with their conduct and draw near to listen, for that is better than when fools offer a sacrifice.

questions.q: Why should people let their words be few?
questions.a: Because God is the eternal God in heaven and people are created by God, so they should think very carefully and not speak rashly or hastily before God.

questions.q: What does a fool do when he talks?
questions.a: A fool talks with many words.

questions.q: What should a person do after he vows a vow to God?
questions.a: He should fulfill it without delay.

questions.q: What is better for a person to do than to make a vow that he does not carry out?
questions.a: It is better for a person not to make a vow than to make a vow that he does not carry out.

questions.q: What might God do if a person’s words cause him to sin?
questions.a: God might become angry and destroy the work of that person’s hands.

questions.q: What should a person do instead of chasing many words and empty things?
questions.a: He should fear God.

questions.q: Why should someone not be astonished when he sees the poor being oppressed and robbed of just and fair treatment?
questions.a: He should not be astonished because the people who could hold the powerful to account see the injustice and do nothing about it.

questions.q: Who eats from what the fields produce?
questions.a: Important people and even the king eat from what the fields produce.

questions.q: What happens to a person who loves silver?
questions.a: A person who loves silver will never be satisfied no matter how much they have.

questions.q: What happens as prosperity increases?
questions.a: As prosperity increases, so also do the people who consume it.

questions.q: What does not allow a rich person to sleep well?
questions.a: The wealth of a rich person does not allow him to sleep well.

questions.q: What misfortune did Qoheleth see concerning wealth?
questions.a: He saw wealth kept by its owner that ended up harming him.

questions.q: What happens when the rich man loses his wealth through misfortune?
questions.a: When the rich man loses his wealth through misfortune, he has nothing left to give to the son he fathered.

questions.q: How is a man born and how will he leave this life?
questions.a: A man is born naked from his mother’s womb and possessing nothing, so also, he will leave this life without taking anything he possesses.

questions.q: What profit does a person gain from laboring as if for the wind?
questions.a: He gains no profit; it is a sickening misfortune.

questions.q: According to the Teacher, how does the man who lost his wealth spend all his days?
questions.a: He spends all his days in darkness, greatly troubled, sick, and angry.

questions.q: What did Qoheleth say is good for a person to do?
questions.a: He said it is good to eat, drink, and find satisfaction in one’s hard work during the life that God has given him.

questions.q: What does Qoheleth call the ability to enjoy the wealth God gives?
questions.a: He calls it a gift of God.

questions.q: Why does a person not call to mind very often the days of his life?
questions.a: A person does not call to mind very often the days of his life, because God makes him keep busy with the things that he enjoys doing.

commentary.text: What renders devotion vain. (Eccl. 5:1-3) Of vows, and oppression. (Eccl. 5:4-8) the vanity of riches shown. (Eccl. 5:9-7) The right use of riches. (Eccl. 5:18-20)

Eccl. 5:1-3 Address thyself to the worship of God, and take time to compose thyself for it. Keep thy thoughts from roving and wandering: keep thy affections from running out toward wrong objects. We should avoid vain repetitions; copious prayers are not here condemned, but those that are unmeaning. How often our wandering thoughts render attendance on Divine ordinances little better than the sacrifice of fools! Many words and hasty ones, used in prayer, show folly in the heart, low thoughts of God, and careless thoughts of our own souls.

Eccl. 5:4-8 When a person made engagements rashly, he suffered his mouth to cause his flesh to sin. The case supposes a man coming to the priest, and pretending that his vow was made rashly, and that it would be wrong to fulfil it. Such mockery of God would bring the Divine displeasure, which might blast what was thus unduly kept. We are to keep down the fear of man. Set God before thee; then, if thou seest the oppression of the poor, thou wilt not find fault with Divine Providence; nor think the worse of the institution of magistracy, when thou seest the ends of it thus perverted; nor of religion, when thou seest it will not secure men from suffering wrong. But though oppressors may be secure, God will reckon for all.

Eccl. 5:9-17 The goodness of Providence is more equally distributed than appears to a careless observer. The king needs the common things of life, and the poor share them; they relish their morsel better than he does his luxuries. There are bodily desires which silver itself will not satisfy, much less will worldly abundance satisfy spiritual desires. The more men have, the better house they must keep, the more servants they must employ, the more guests they must entertain, and the more they will have hanging on them. The sleep of the labourer is sweet, not only because he is tired, but because he has little care to break his sleep. The sleep of the diligent Christian, and his long sleep, are sweet; having spent himself and his time in the service of God, he can cheerfully repose in God as his Rest. But those who have every thing else, often fail to secure a good night's sleep; their abundance breaks their rest. Riches do hurt, and draw away the heart from God and duty. Men do hurt with their riches, not only gratifying their own lusts, but oppressing others, and dealing hardly with them. They will see that they have laboured for the wind, when, at death, they find the profit of their labour is all gone like the wind, they know not whither. How ill the covetous worldling bears the calamities of human life! He does not sorrow to repentance, but is angry at the providence of God, angry at all about him; which doubles his affliction.

Eccl. 5:18-20 Life is God's gift. We must not view our calling as a drudgery, but take pleasure in the calling where God puts us. A cheerful spirit is a great blessing; it makes employments easy, and afflictions light. Having made a proper use of riches, a man will remember the days of his past life with pleasure. The manner in which Solomon refers to God as the Giver, both of life and its enjoyments, shows they ought to be received and to be used, consistently with his will, and to his glory. Let this passage recommend to all the kind words of the merciful Redeemer, "Labour not for the meat that perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life." Christ is the Bread of life, the only food of the soul. All are invited to partake of this heavenly provision.
